ground_truth: Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm whose running time depends on the balance of partitioning. In the worst case, it runs in Θ(n²), when the partition produces subproblems of sizes n−1 and 0. Under the assumption that all elements are distinct and all permutations are equally likely, its expected running time is Θ(n log n). The algorithm sorts in place and uses additional space proportional to the recursion depth.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, pp. 182–184.
strategic_misconception_explanation: It incorrectly states that the worst-case scenario occurs when the pivot divides the list into two nearly equal sublists. In reality, equal partitioning leads to the best-case (O(n log n)) performance, while the worst-case (O(n^2)) occurs when partitions are maximally unbalanced (sizes n-1 and 0).

ground_truth: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem on a weighted directed graph with nonnegative edge weights. It maintains a set of vertices whose shortest-path distances from the source have been finalized and repeatedly selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance using a priority queue, then relaxes its outgoing edges. Correctness relies on the property that once a vertex is extracted, its shortest-path distance is final, which holds only when all edge weights are nonnegative.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Section 22.3, pp 604 - 645.

ground_truth: Dynamic programming solves optimization problems by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems, typically using a bottom-up approach. A greedy algorithm constructs a solution by repeatedly making the locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of reaching a global optimum. Unlike dynamic programming, greedy algorithms do not rely on solutions to subproblems. Greedy algorithms do not always produce optimal solutions.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 14, pp. 365–370,  Chapter 15, pp. 424, 427.

ground_truth: A hash table maps keys to array slots. A collision occurs when two or more keys hash to the same slot. The load factor α = N/M is the ratio of stored elements to table size. As α increases, the probability of collisions increases and performance degrades. Under uniform hashing and open addressing, the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is approximately 1/(1−α).
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 11, pp 272 - 311.

concept: Binary search tree balancing (AVL vs Red-Black)
ground_truth: An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. This strict balance ensures O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, but may require more rotations during updates. A red-black tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains balance using color-based properties (red and black nodes), guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, typically with fewer rotations than AVL trees at the cost of a potentially higher tree height.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. AVL trees: Problem 13-3, pp. 358–360. Red-black trees: Chapter 13, pp. 331–359.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation states that rotations are performed when the balance factor is >= 2 or <= -2. In AVL trees, the strict definition requires the balance factor to be in {-1, 0, 1}, meaning rotations are triggered when the factor becomes 2 or -2 (i.e., the difference is exactly 2). While 'greater than or equal to 2' is technically true for the trigger condition (since it can't be 3 in a valid AVL tree before rotation), it implies a tolerance that doesn't exist. More critically, it omits the specific AVL property that the height difference must be *at most one*, instead focusing on the violation threshold. However, the most significant error is in the Red-Black section: it lists 'Nodes as seen from the root... contain the same number of black nodes' as a rule. This is incorrect; the rule is that every path from a node to its descendant leaves has the same number of black nodes (Black-Height property), not that all nodes at a certain depth or 'seen from the root' have the same count. This is a fundamental misunderstanding of the property.

concept: Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) - memory consumption
ground_truth: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue to maintain the frontier. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|), as the queue may store up to all vertices in the worst case. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|) in the worst case due to the recursion stack or explicit stack.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. Chapter 20, pp. 549–584.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy of a 'basket' for BFS implies a fixed-size buffer or sliding window, which misleads learners into thinking BFS has bounded memory usage or uses a queue with limited capacity, whereas BFS requires a queue that can grow up to O(V).

ground_truth: Space complexity measures the amount of memory required by an algorithm as a function of input size, including both input storage and auxiliary space used during execution. Algorithm design often involves trade-offs between time and space, where additional memory can be used to improve running time (e.g., storing intermediate results), while reducing memory usage may increase running time.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 1, pp. 5–16.

ground_truth: Inheritance is a mechanism in object-oriented programming that allows a class (subtype) to inherit properties and behavior from another class (base type), enabling code reuse and hierarchical relationships. The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. This requires that inherited behavior is preserved, including method contracts, invariants, and preconditions/postconditions.
reference: Liskov, B. H.; Wing, J. M. (1994). "A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping". ACM TOPLAS, 16(6), pp. 1811–1841. / Martin, R. C. (2017). Clean Architecture. Prentice Hall. pp. 140-145

ground_truth: An interface defines a type by specifying a set of methods that a class must implement, without requiring instance state, while an abstract class can provide both method implementations and instance fields. Interfaces enable multiple inheritance of type, whereas abstract classes support code reuse through shared implementation but allow only single inheritance. Interfaces are generally preferred for defining types, while abstract classes are useful when sharing common code among closely related classes.
reference: Bloch, J. (2018). Effective Java (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley, Item 20, pp. 99–107.

ground_truth: Lexical scope means that scope is defined by author-time decisions of where functions are declared. The lexing phase of compilation is able to know where and how all identifiers are declared, and thus predict how they will be looked up during execution. Closure is when a function is able to remember and access its lexical scope even when that function is executing outside its lexical scope.
reference: Simpson, K. (2014). You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures. O'Reilly Media, Chapter 2 (Lexical Scope) and Chapter 5 (Scope Closure), pp 47-52.

ground_truth: Static typing performs type checking at compile time, using static analysis of the program to approximate runtime behavior and detect type errors before execution. Dynamic typing performs type checking at runtime, where variables are not bound to fixed types and type errors are detected during program execution. Type safety is the property that well-typed programs do not produce undefined or invalid behavior, such as applying operations to incompatible types.
reference: Pierce, B. C. (2002). Types and Programming Languages. MIT Press, Chapter 1: Introduction.

ground_truth: Use checked exceptions for conditions from which the caller can reasonably be expected to recover. Use runtime exceptions (unchecked) to indicate programming errors, typically precondition violations where the client failed to adhere to the API's contract. Errors are reserved for JVM-level failures and should not be caught or subclassed.

strategic_misconception_explanation: It incorrectly classifies `ArithmeticException` as a checked exception and `FileNotFoundException` as an unchecked exception, reversing their actual status in Java.

ground_truth: Reference counting associates a count of references with each object and reclaims memory when the count reaches zero, but it cannot collect cyclic garbage. The mark-and-sweep algorithm identifies reachable objects by tracing from root references, marks all reachable objects, and reclaims memory occupied by unmarked objects. Unlike reference counting, mark-and-sweep can collect cyclic garbage because it determines reachability through graph traversal rather than reference counts.
reference: Jones, R.; Hosking, A.; Moss, E. (2023). The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management (2nd ed.). CRC Press, Chapter 2 (Mark-Sweep) and Chapter 5 (Reference Counting).

ground_truth: Multithreading is a form of concurrency that uses multiple threads of execution managed by the operating system to perform tasks in parallel or overlapping time periods. Asynchronous programming is a form of concurrency in which operations are executed without blocking the calling thread, typically by representing ongoing work as tasks that can be awaited or completed later. ground_truth: To preserve data integrity, a database system must ensure: Atomicity—either all operations of a transaction are reflected in the database or none are; Consistency—a committed transaction preserves all defined integrity constraints, moving the database from one valid state to another; Isolation—concurrent transactions execute without interfering with each other, as if executed serially, with intermediate results hidden; Durability—once a transaction commits, its changes persist despite system failures. Consistency refers to maintaining database integrity rules, while Isolation refers to controlling interaction between concurrent transactions.

ground_truth: Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes contain atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups. Second Normal Form (2NF): The relation is in 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): The relation is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies; non-key attributes depend only on candidate keys. Normalization to 3NF eliminates common insertion, update, and deletion anomalies and is widely considered a practical design goal, although higher normal forms (e.g., BCNF) may be required in some cases.
reference: Date, C. J. (2004). An Introduction to Database Systems (8th ed.). Pearson/Addison Wesley, Chapter 12: Further Normalization I: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, pp. 349–388.

ground_truth: The SQL JOIN clause combines rows from two or more tables based on a specified join condition. INNER JOIN returns only rows for which the join condition evaluates to true in both tables. LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the right table are set to NULL. RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the left table are set to NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables; rows are matched where the join condition holds, and non-matching rows from either side are padded with NULL values.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 6.3.6–6.3.8: SQL Join Expressions and Outerjoins.

concept: Indexes: When a B-tree index does not speed up a query
ground_truth: A B-tree index may not be used or may not improve query performance when the query has low selectivity (i.e., it returns a large fraction of the table), in which case a full table scan can be more efficient than index-based access due to the cost of random disk I/O. The index may also be ineffective if the query applies functions, expressions, or negation to the indexed column, preventing efficient index lookup, or if the table is very small. Database query optimizers use cost-based analysis and table statistics to determine whether to use an index.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 14: Index Structures. / Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 14: Indexing.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly claims that an index is ineffective for finding a unique value (high selectivity), whereas indexes are most effective for high selectivity queries. It also fails to mention the actual reasons for index inefficacy (low selectivity, functions on columns, small tables).

ground_truth: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability. Consistency means that all nodes see the same data at the same time (i.e., every read reflects the most recent write). Availability means that every request receives a response, regardless of the state of individual nodes. Partition tolerance means that the system continues to operate despite network partitions (communication failures between nodes). Since network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, CAP is commonly interpreted as a trade-off between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) under partition conditions.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 19: Distributed Databases.

concept: Denormalization: When and why to use it
ground_truth: Denormalization is the process of intentionally introducing redundancy into a normalized relational schema to improve read performance by reducing the need for join operations. It is a deliberate trade-off, commonly used in read-heavy workloads (e.g., reporting or data warehousing), where the cost of joins outweighs the overhead of maintaining redundant data. While denormalization can significantly accelerate SELECT queries, it increases storage requirements, complicates write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and introduces the risk of data inconsistency due to redundant representations.

ground_truth: The TCP three-way handshake establishes a connection and synchronizes sequence numbers between client and server. (1) The client sends a TCP segment with the SYN flag set and a pseudo-random initial sequence number (client_isn), entering the SYN_SENT state. (2) The server responds with a SYN-ACK segment containing its own pseudo-random initial sequence number (server_isn) and an acknowledgment number of client_isn+1, entering the SYN_RCVD state. (3) The client replies with an ACK segment with acknowledgment number server_isn+1. Both sides then transition to the ESTABLISHED state. The handshake confirms bidirectional communication and initializes sequence number spaces for reliable data transfer.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 3.5: TCP Connection Management, pp. 240–246.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation states that the initial SYN packet includes an acknowledgment number set to 0. In the TCP specification, the ACK flag is not set in the initial SYN packet, so the acknowledgment number field is technically undefined or ignored by the receiver, rather than being explicitly set to 0 as a valid acknowledgment of prior data.

concept: OSI model vs TCP/IP model (differences in layers)
ground_truth: The OSI model defines a seven-layer architecture: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application. The TCP/IP model defines a four-layer architecture: Link (Network Interface), Internet, Transport, and Application. The TCP/IP model consolidates the OSI Physical and Data Link layers into the Link layer, and the OSI Session and Presentation layers into the Application layer. While the OSI model serves as a conceptual reference framework, the TCP/IP model reflects the practical architecture of the Internet protocol suite.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 1.5
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation lists five layers for the TCP/IP model (Shoreline, Beach, Surf Zone, Wave Break, Seaside Resorts), whereas the TCP/IP model is defined as having four layers. This is a factual error regarding the structure of the model.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy introduces a 'Wave Break' layer which does not exist in the standard TCP/IP model, potentially confusing the learner about the number of layers or the specific function of the Internet layer.

ground_truth: DNS resolution can be recursive or iterative. In recursive resolution, a DNS server resolves the query on behalf of the client, contacting other servers as needed and returning the final answer. In iterative resolution, each DNS server returns the best information it has (often a referral), and the client (or resolver) continues querying other servers. Recursive queries shift the resolution burden to the server, while iterative queries distribute it across multiple queries.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson,Chapter 2.4: DNS, pp. 168–175.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy for recursive resolution states the friend 'goes to ask someone else until they find out,' which implies the friend performs the iterative steps. In reality, recursive resolution means the friend returns the final answer without the client knowing the intermediate steps. While the explanation later says 'your computer asks different DNS servers one by one' for recursive, which is technically the definition of iterative resolution from the client's perspective (or a stub resolver doing recursion), the analogy itself is slightly confused. However, the text explicitly corrects this by saying 'Your computer asks different DNS servers one by one' for recursive, which is actually a description of iterative resolution (or the stub resolver acting as a recursive client). Wait, let's look closer. 'Your computer asks different DNS servers one by one until it finds the correct IP address' describes iterative resolution. The label 'Recursive DNS resolution' is applied to this description. This is a fundamental error in defining the terms. Recursive resolution is when the *server* does the work. Iterative is when the *client* does the work. Explanation 1 swaps the definitions or describes iterative behavior under the label of recursive. Specifically, it says for Recursive: 'Your computer asks different DNS servers one by one'. This is false; in recursive resolution, the client asks *one* server, and that server asks others. The client does not ask 'different DNS servers one by one'. This is a strategic misconception.

Routers use the longest prefix match rule to determine the forwarding path for a packet.

concept: HTTP methods: Idempotency of GET, PUT, DELETE versus POST
ground_truth: HTTP methods differ in semantics and idempotency. A method is idempotent if multiple identical requests have the same effect as a single request. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeated requests do not change the result beyond the initial application. POST is not idempotent, as repeated requests can create multiple resources or cause repeated side effects. Idempotency is important for reliability and retry mechanisms in distributed systems.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 2.2: The Web and HTTP, pp. 122–130.

POST is not idempotent, as repeated requests can create multiple resources or cause repeated side effects. Idempotency is important for reliability and retry mechanisms in distributed systems.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 2.2: The Web and HTTP, pp. 122–130.

concept: Routing: Distance Vector (RIP) vs Link State (OSPF)
ground_truth: Distance-vector routing algorithms (e.g., RIP) compute shortest paths based on information from neighboring routers, iteratively updating distance estimates using distributed Bellman-Ford equations. Link-state routing algorithms (e.g., OSPF) require each router to have a complete view of the network topology and compute shortest paths using Dijkstra’s algorithm. Distance-vector approaches are simpler but slower to converge and susceptible to routing loops, while link-state approaches converge faster and provide more accurate routing at the cost of higher complexity.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 5.3–5.4: Routing Algorithms, pp. 365–385.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy implies OSPF routers calculate paths 'without asking anyone else for help' because they have a map. This is misleading because OSPF routers must actively exchange Link State Advertisements (LSAs) with neighbors to build that map; they do not possess the topology inherently or without communication.

concept: TLS handshake (RSA vs Diffie-Hellman key exchange)
ground_truth: TLS handshake protocols establish a secure connection by negotiating cryptographic parameters and exchanging keys. In RSA-based key exchange, the client encrypts a premaster secret with the server’s public key, allowing the server to derive the session keys. In Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, both parties contribute to a shared secret without transmitting it directly, providing forward secrecy. Modern TLS implementations prefer (EC)DHE over RSA key exchange due to improved security properties.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 8.3: Secure Sockets Layer / TLS, pp. 712–720.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly states that RSA involves exchanging a password in person and implies the private key is used for encryption in the context of the analogy, while also misrepresenting the role of the 'magical third party' in DH as a key distributor rather than a mathematical protocol for deriving a shared secret without transmission.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy of a 'magical third party' for Diffie-Hellman is dangerous because it implies a trusted third party is required to generate or provide the secret, whereas DH is specifically designed to allow two parties to generate a shared secret without any prior shared secrets or trusted third parties.

ground_truth: A process is a program in execution with its own memory space, resources, and execution context. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process that shares the same address space and resources but has its own program counter, registers, and stack. Threads within the same process can communicate more efficiently than separate processes due to shared memory.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts (10th ed.), Chapter 4: Threads, pp. 163–172.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly states that 'threads are managed by the operating system's kernel, whereas processes are managed by the user-level libraries or the OS itself.' In standard OS theory, both processes and threads are kernel-managed entities (in kernel-level threading models, which is the standard context for this comparison). While user-level threads exist, stating that processes are managed by user-level libraries is factually incorrect regarding the fundamental definition of a process.

ground_truth: Context switching is the process of saving the state of a currently running process or thread and restoring the state of another, enabling multitasking. The operating system saves CPU registers, program counter, and memory mapping information of the current process and loads the corresponding state of the next scheduled process.

dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy implies that context switching requires starting tasks 'from scratch' (dropping balls and picking them up again), which contradicts the core definition of context switching as saving and restoring state to resume exactly where left off.

SJF selects the process with the shortest expected CPU burst time, minimizing average waiting time but risking starvation. Round Robin assigns a fixed time quantum to each process, ensuring fairness and responsiveness in time-sharing systems.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Chapter 5: CPU Scheduling, pp. 198–210.

Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical units such as functions or data structures, improving logical organization but suffering from external fragmentation. Modern systems often combine both approaches.

A counting semaphore allows multiple concurrent accesses up to a defined limit, while a binary semaphore (mutex) allows only one. Semaphores prevent race conditions by enforcing mutual exclusion and coordination between concurrent processes.

ground_truth: Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm whose running time depends on the balance of partitioning. In the worst case, it runs in Θ(n²), when the partition produces subproblems of sizes n−1 and 0. Under the assumption that all elements are distinct and all permutations are equally likely, its expected running time is Θ(n log n). The algorithm sorts in place and uses additional space proportional to the recursion depth.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, pp. 182–184.

ground_truth: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem on a weighted directed graph with nonnegative edge weights. It maintains a set of vertices whose shortest-path distances from the source have been finalized and repeatedly selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance using a priority queue, then relaxes its outgoing edges. Correctness relies on the property that once a vertex is extracted, its shortest-path distance is final, which holds only when all edge weights are nonnegative.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Section 22.3, pp 604 - 645.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation states that 'the algorithm stops when it finds the first path, assuming it's the shortest.' This is factually incorrect; Dijkstra's algorithm continues until all reachable nodes are finalized or the target is reached, but the core failure with negative weights is that the *finalized* distances are incorrect, not that it stops prematurely. It implies a termination error rather than a correctness error.

ground_truth: Dynamic programming solves optimization problems by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems, typically using a bottom-up approach. A greedy algorithm constructs a solution by repeatedly making the locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of reaching a global optimum. Unlike dynamic programming, greedy algorithms do not rely on solutions to subproblems. Greedy algorithms do not always produce optimal solutions.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 14, pp. 365–370,  Chapter 15, pp. 424, 427.

concept: Binary search tree balancing (AVL vs Red-Black)
ground_truth: An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. This strict balance ensures O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, but may require more rotations during updates. A red-black tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains balance using color-based properties (red and black nodes), guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, typically with fewer rotations than AVL trees at the cost of a potentially higher tree height.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. AVL trees: Problem 13-3, pp. 358–360. Red-black trees: Chapter 13, pp. 331–359.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation states that AVL trees require the left and right sides to be the 'exact same height' for the tallest parts. This is factually incorrect; AVL trees allow a height difference of at most 1, not 0. This misconception could lead a learner to believe AVL trees are perfectly balanced (like a complete binary tree) rather than strictly height-balanced.

concept: Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) - memory consumption
ground_truth: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue to maintain the frontier. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|), as the queue may store up to all vertices in the worst case. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|) in the worst case due to the recursion stack or explicit stack.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. Chapter 20, pp. 549–584.

ground_truth: Space complexity measures the amount of memory required by an algorithm as a function of input size, including both input storage and auxiliary space used during execution. Algorithm design often involves trade-offs between time and space, where additional memory can be used to improve running time (e.g., storing intermediate results), while reducing memory usage may increase running time.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 1, pp. 5–16.

ground_truth: Inheritance is a mechanism in object-oriented programming that allows a class (subtype) to inherit properties and behavior from another class (base type), enabling code reuse and hierarchical relationships. The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. This requires that inherited behavior is preserved, including method contracts, invariants, and preconditions/postconditions.
reference: Liskov, B. H.; Wing, J. M. (1994). "A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping". ACM TOPLAS, 16(6), pp. 1811–1841. / Martin, R. C. (2017). Clean Architecture. Prentice Hall. pp. 140-145

ground_truth: An interface defines a type by specifying a set of methods that a class must implement, without requiring instance state, while an abstract class can provide both method implementations and instance fields. Interfaces enable multiple inheritance of type, whereas abstract classes support code reuse through shared implementation but allow only single inheritance. Interfaces are generally preferred for defining types, while abstract classes are useful when sharing common code among closely related classes.
reference: Bloch, J. (2018). Effective Java (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley, Item 20, pp. 99–107.

ground_truth: Lexical scope means that scope is defined by author-time decisions of where functions are declared. The lexing phase of compilation is able to know where and how all identifiers are declared, and thus predict how they will be looked up during execution. Closure is when a function is able to remember and access its lexical scope even when that function is executing outside its lexical scope.
reference: Simpson, K. (2014). You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures. O'Reilly Media, Chapter 2 (Lexical Scope) and Chapter 5 (Scope Closure), pp 47-52.

ground_truth: Static typing performs type checking at compile time, using static analysis of the program to approximate runtime behavior and detect type errors before execution. Dynamic typing performs type checking at runtime, where variables are not bound to fixed types and type errors are detected during program execution. Type safety is the property that well-typed programs do not produce undefined or invalid behavior, such as applying operations to incompatible types.
reference: Pierce, B. C. (2002). Types and Programming Languages. MIT Press, Chapter 1: Introduction.

ground_truth: Use checked exceptions for conditions from which the caller can reasonably be expected to recover. Use runtime exceptions (unchecked) to indicate programming errors, typically precondition violations where the client failed to adhere to the API's contract. Errors are reserved for JVM-level failures and should not be caught or subclassed.
reference: Bloch, J. (2018). Effective Java (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley, Item 70, pp. 297–300.

ground_truth: Reference counting associates a count of references with each object and reclaims memory when the count reaches zero, but it cannot collect cyclic garbage. The mark-and-sweep algorithm identifies reachable objects by tracing from root references, marks all reachable objects, and reclaims memory occupied by unmarked objects. Unlike reference counting, mark-and-sweep can collect cyclic garbage because it determines reachability through graph traversal rather than reference counts.
reference: Jones, R.; Hosking, A.; Moss, E. (2023). The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management (2nd ed.). CRC Press, Chapter 2 (Mark-Sweep) and Chapter 5 (Reference Counting).

ground_truth: Multithreading is a form of concurrency that uses multiple threads of execution managed by the operating system to perform tasks in parallel or overlapping time periods. Asynchronous programming is a form of concurrency in which operations are executed without blocking the calling thread, typically by representing ongoing work as tasks that can be awaited or completed later. Unlike multithreading, asynchronous programming does not require a dedicated thread for each concurrent operation.
reference: Cleary, S. (2019). Concurrency in C# Cookbook (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media, Chapter 1.

ground_truth: To preserve data integrity, a database system must ensure: Atomicity—either all operations of a transaction are reflected in the database or none are; Consistency—a committed transaction preserves all defined integrity constraints, moving the database from one valid state to another; Isolation—concurrent transactions execute without interfering with each other, as if executed serially, with intermediate results hidden; Durability—once a transaction commits, its changes persist despite system failures. Consistency refers to maintaining database integrity rules, while Isolation refers to controlling interaction between concurrent transactions.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 17: Transactions.

strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly attributes 'dirty reads' to a lack of Isolation in the 'Why ACID Matters' section. A dirty read occurs when a transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction; this is prevented by Isolation. The text lists 'Dirty Reads' under the consequences of chaos without ACID, but then defines Isolation as preventing dirty reads later. However, in the 'Why ACID Matters' list, it conflates 'Inconsistency' (reading uncommitted data) with the result of Inconsistency. More critically, it states 'Inconsistency: One transaction might read data modified by another transaction before that other transaction is finished'. This describes a dirty read or non-repeatable read, which is an Isolation failure, not a Consistency failure. Consistency is about rules/constraints, not visibility. The text then says 'Isolation... prevents dirty reads'. This is correct. Wait, let's re-read carefully. Under 'Why ACID Matters', it lists 'Inconsistency' as reading data modified by another before it's finished. This is technically an Isolation issue (specifically, lack of isolation levels). Then it lists 'Dirty Reads' separately. This is confusing and potentially misleading because it labels an Isolation failure as 'Inconsistency'. However, in the 'Focusing on Consistency vs Isolation' section, it correctly distinguishes them: Consistency is about rules, Isolation is about visibility. The initial list is sloppy but the core definition is correct. Is it a strategic misconception? It suggests that reading uncommitted data is an 'Inconsistency' problem. In database theory, this is an Isolation problem. The final state might be consistent, but the intermediate state was visible. Labeling the *act* of reading uncommitted data as 'Inconsistency' is a category error. It should be labeled 'Isolation violation'. This is a subtle but significant error in terminology.

ground_truth: Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes contain atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups. Second Normal Form (2NF): The relation is in 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): The relation is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies; non-key attributes depend only on candidate keys. Normalization to 3NF eliminates common insertion, update, and deletion anomalies and is widely considered a practical design goal, although higher normal forms (e.g., BCNF) may be required in some cases.
reference: Date, C. J. (2004). An Introduction to Database Systems (8th ed.). Pearson/Addison Wesley, Chapter 12: Further Normalization I: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, pp. 349–388.

ground_truth: The SQL JOIN clause combines rows from two or more tables based on a specified join condition. INNER JOIN returns only rows for which the join condition evaluates to true in both tables. LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the right table are set to NULL. RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the left table are set to NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables; rows are matched where the join condition holds, and non-matching rows from either side are padded with NULL values.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 6.3.6–6.3.8: SQL Join Expressions and Outerjoins.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation contains a significant factual error in the SQL examples for LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL JOINs. It claims that a LEFT JOIN on `authors` and `books` will include an author with ID 105 who does not exist in the `authors` table. A LEFT JOIN preserves rows from the *left* table (`authors`); it cannot create rows for entities that do not exist in that table. The row for ID 105 appears in the `books` table, so it would only appear in a RIGHT JOIN (on `books`) or FULL JOIN, not a LEFT JOIN on `authors`. Similarly, the RIGHT JOIN example incorrectly shows all books with NULL authors at the top and matching authors at the bottom, implying a specific ordering or behavior that isn't standard, and more importantly, the logic is confused regarding which table drives the inclusion. The most critical error is the LEFT JOIN result set including a non-existent author.

concept: Indexes: When a B-tree index does not speed up a query
ground_truth: A B-tree index may not be used or may not improve query performance when the query has low selectivity (i.e., it returns a large fraction of the table), in which case a full table scan can be more efficient than index-based access due to the cost of random disk I/O. The index may also be ineffective if the query applies functions, expressions, or negation to the indexed column, preventing efficient index lookup, or if the table is very small. Database query optimizers use cost-based analysis and table statistics to determine whether to use an index.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 14: Index Structures. / Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 14: Indexing.

While B-trees *can* handle ranges, the explanation frames these as fundamental limitations where the index 'doesn't help', which is misleading. B-trees are specifically designed to handle range queries efficiently. Saying they 'don't help' for finding the next page in a sequence (range scan) is factually incorrect regarding B-tree capabilities. It also conflates 'not speeding up' with 'not helping at all'.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy of the index being a list of words to pages is good for equality, but the claim that it doesn't help for 'finding the next page' (range) is a misleading analogy for a B-tree, which is ordered and excels at ranges. This leads to the wrong belief that B-trees cannot efficiently handle range queries.

concept: Transactions: Different isolation levels (Read Committed vs Serializable)
ground_truth: READ COMMITTED ensures that a transaction reads only data that has been committed by other transactions; however, successive reads within the same transaction may return different results, allowing non-repeatable reads and phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE ensures that concurrent transactions execute with results equivalent to some serial schedule, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation levels improve correctness guarantees but typically reduce concurrency.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 17: Transactions.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly states that Read Committed 'prevents phantoms under some definitions' in the summary, whereas the reference definition and standard theory state that Read Committed allows phantom reads. Additionally, it claims Serializable prevents seeing 'data from other committed changes happening during your transaction,' which is technically inaccurate for standard Serializable isolation (which allows seeing committed changes made before the transaction started, just not new ones inserted during the transaction in a way that affects the current read scope, but the key is that it prevents phantoms, not that it hides all concurrent committed data). However, the most significant error is the claim about Read Committed preventing phantoms in the summary.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy for Serializable ('Each Cook Has Their Own Private Kitchen') implies that you cannot see *any* data changes happening while you are working, including committed ones. In reality, Serializable transactions can see data committed by other transactions before they started. The analogy suggests a snapshot isolation or strict two-phase locking that hides all concurrent updates, which is misleading about the visibility of committed data.

concept: Transactions: Different isolation levels (Read Committed vs Serializable)
ground_truth: READ COMMITTED ensures that a transaction reads only data that has been committed by other transactions; however, successive reads within the same transaction may return different results, allowing non-repeatable reads and phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE ensures that concurrent transactions execute with results equivalent to some serial schedule, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation levels improve correctness guarantees but typically reduce concurrency.

ground_truth: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability. Consistency means that all nodes see the same data at the same time (i.e., every read reflects the most recent write). Availability means that every request receives a response, regardless of the state of individual nodes. Partition tolerance means that the system continues to operate despite network partitions (communication failures between nodes). Since network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, CAP is commonly interpreted as a trade-off between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) under partition conditions.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 19: Distributed Databases.

concept: Denormalization: When and why to use it
ground_truth: Denormalization is the process of intentionally introducing redundancy into a normalized relational schema to improve read performance by reducing the need for join operations. It is a deliberate trade-off, commonly used in read-heavy workloads (e.g., reporting or data warehousing), where the cost of joins outweighs the overhead of maintaining redundant data. While denormalization can significantly accelerate SELECT queries, it increases storage requirements, complicates write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and introduces the risk of data inconsistency due to redundant representations.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson. / Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill.

ground_truth: The TCP three-way handshake establishes a connection and synchronizes sequence numbers between client and server. (1) The client sends a TCP segment with the SYN flag set and a pseudo-random initial sequence number (client_isn), entering the SYN_SENT state. (2) The server responds with a SYN-ACK segment containing its own pseudo-random initial sequence number (server_isn) and an acknowledgment number of client_isn+1, entering the SYN_RCVD state. (3) The client replies with an ACK segment with acknowledgment number server_isn+1. Both sides then transition to the ESTABLISHED state. The handshake confirms bidirectional communication and initializes sequence number spaces for reliable data transfer.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 3.5: TCP Connection Management, pp. 240–246.

concept: OSI model vs TCP/IP model (differences in layers)
ground_truth: The OSI model defines a seven-layer architecture: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application. The TCP/IP model defines a four-layer architecture: Link (Network Interface), Internet, Transport, and Application. The TCP/IP model consolidates the OSI Physical and Data Link layers into the Link layer, and the OSI Session and Presentation layers into the Application layer. While the OSI model serves as a conceptual reference framework, the TCP/IP model reflects the practical architecture of the Internet protocol suite.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 1.5
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly maps the OSI layers to the TCP/IP layers. It states that the TCP/IP Application layer corresponds to OSI Application + Presentation, and the Transport layer corresponds to Session + Transport. In reality, the TCP/IP Application layer encompasses OSI Application, Presentation, and Session layers. The Session and Presentation functions are not part of the TCP/IP Transport layer.

ground_truth: DNS resolution can be recursive or iterative. In recursive resolution, a DNS server resolves the query on behalf of the client, contacting other servers as needed and returning the final answer. In iterative resolution, each DNS server returns the best information it has (often a referral), and the client (or resolver) continues querying other servers. Recursive queries shift the resolution burden to the server, while iterative queries distribute it across multiple queries.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson,Chapter 2.4: DNS, pp. 168–175.

ground_truth: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) represents IP addresses using a prefix of arbitrary length, written as a.b.c.d/x, where x indicates the number of bits in the network portion. CIDR enables flexible subnetting and efficient allocation of IP address space by eliminating fixed class boundaries. Routers use the longest prefix match rule to determine the forwarding path for a packet.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 4.4: IP Addressing, pp. 330–336

concept: HTTP methods: Idempotency of GET, PUT, DELETE versus POST
ground_truth: HTTP methods differ in semantics and idempotency. A method is idempotent if multiple identical requests have the same effect as a single request. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeated requests do not change the result beyond the initial application. POST is not idempotent, as repeated requests can create multiple resources or cause repeated side effects. Idempotency is important for reliability and retry mechanisms in distributed systems.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 2.2: The Web and HTTP, pp. 122–130.

concept: Routing: Distance Vector (RIP) vs Link State (OSPF)
ground_truth: Distance-vector routing algorithms (e.g., RIP) compute shortest paths based on information from neighboring routers, iteratively updating distance estimates using distributed Bellman-Ford equations. Link-state routing algorithms (e.g., OSPF) require each router to have a complete view of the network topology and compute shortest paths using Dijkstra’s algorithm. Distance-vector approaches are simpler but slower to converge and susceptible to routing loops, while link-state approaches converge faster and provide more accurate routing at the cost of higher complexity.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 5.3–5.4: Routing Algorithms, pp. 365–385.

concept: TLS handshake (RSA vs Diffie-Hellman key exchange)
ground_truth: TLS handshake protocols establish a secure connection by negotiating cryptographic parameters and exchanging keys. In RSA-based key exchange, the client encrypts a premaster secret with the server’s public key, allowing the server to derive the session keys. In Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, both parties contribute to a shared secret without transmitting it directly, providing forward secrecy. Modern TLS implementations prefer (EC)DHE over RSA key exchange due to improved security properties.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 8.3: Secure Sockets Layer / TLS, pp. 712–720.

ground_truth: Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm whose running time depends on the balance of partitioning. In the worst case, it runs in Θ(n²), when the partition produces subproblems of sizes n−1 and 0. Under the assumption that all elements are distinct and all permutations are equally likely, its expected running time is Θ(n log n). The algorithm sorts in place and uses additional space proportional to the recursion depth.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, pp. 182–184.

ground_truth: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem on a weighted directed graph with nonnegative edge weights. It maintains a set of vertices whose shortest-path distances from the source have been finalized and repeatedly selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance using a priority queue, then relaxes its outgoing edges. Correctness relies on the property that once a vertex is extracted, its shortest-path distance is final, which holds only when all edge weights are nonnegative.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Section 22.3, pp 604 - 645.

ground_truth: Dynamic programming solves optimization problems by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems, typically using a bottom-up approach. A greedy algorithm constructs a solution by repeatedly making the locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of reaching a global optimum. Unlike dynamic programming, greedy algorithms do not rely on solutions to subproblems. Greedy algorithms do not always produce optimal solutions.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 14, pp. 365–370,  Chapter 15, pp. 424, 427.

ground_truth: A hash table maps keys to array slots. A collision occurs when two or more keys hash to the same slot. The load factor α = N/M is the ratio of stored elements to table size. As α increases, the probability of collisions increases and performance degrades. Under uniform hashing and open addressing, the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is approximately 1/(1−α).
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 11, pp 272 - 311.

concept: Binary search tree balancing (AVL vs Red-Black)
ground_truth: An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. This strict balance ensures O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, but may require more rotations during updates. A red-black tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains balance using color-based properties (red and black nodes), guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, typically with fewer rotations than AVL trees at the cost of a potentially higher tree height.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. AVL trees: Problem 13-3, pp. 358–360. Red-black trees: Chapter 13, pp. 331–359.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy states that in an AVL tree, 'left and right sides always equal'. This is factually incorrect; AVL trees allow a height difference of at most 1, not 0. This misconception could lead a learner to believe AVL trees are perfectly symmetric, which is a stricter and different condition than height-balanced.

concept: Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) - memory consumption
ground_truth: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue to maintain the frontier. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|), as the queue may store up to all vertices in the worst case. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. Its auxiliary space complexity is O(|V|) in the worst case due to the recursion stack or explicit stack.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. Chapter 20, pp. 549–584.

ground_truth: Inheritance is a mechanism in object-oriented programming that allows a class (subtype) to inherit properties and behavior from another class (base type), enabling code reuse and hierarchical relationships. The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. This requires that inherited behavior is preserved, including method contracts, invariants, and preconditions/postconditions.
reference: Liskov, B. H.; Wing, J. M. (1994). "A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping". ACM TOPLAS, 16(6), pp. 1811–1841. / Martin, R. C. (2017). Clean Architecture. Prentice Hall. pp. 140-145

LSP allows for behavioral changes (like returning a more specific type or narrowing preconditions) as long as the contract is preserved. The 'cannot remove' phrasing might mislead learners into thinking overriding methods is forbidden or that behavioral variance is inherently bad, whereas LSP is about substitutability, not rigid identity of behavior.

LSP permits changing behavior (e.g., a Square's area calculation differs from a generic Shape's abstract expectation, or a Dog's bark differs from Animal's generic sound) provided the postconditions and invariants hold. The 'cannot change' rule is too strict and misleading for a precise definition.

ground_truth: An interface defines a type by specifying a set of methods that a class must implement, without requiring instance state, while an abstract class can provide both method implementations and instance fields. Interfaces enable multiple inheritance of type, whereas abstract classes support code reuse through shared implementation but allow only single inheritance. Interfaces are generally preferred for defining types, while abstract classes are useful when sharing common code among closely related classes.
reference: Bloch, J. (2018). Effective Java (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley, Item 20, pp. 99–107.

ground_truth: Reference counting associates a count of references with each object and reclaims memory when the count reaches zero, but it cannot collect cyclic garbage. The mark-and-sweep algorithm identifies reachable objects by tracing from root references, marks all reachable objects, and reclaims memory occupied by unmarked objects. Unlike reference counting, mark-and-sweep can collect cyclic garbage because it determines reachability through graph traversal rather than reference counts.
reference: Jones, R.; Hosking, A.; Moss, E. (2023). The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management (2nd ed.). CRC Press, Chapter 2 (Mark-Sweep) and Chapter 5 (Reference Counting).

ground_truth: Multithreading is a form of concurrency that uses multiple threads of execution managed by the operating system to perform tasks in parallel or overlapping time periods. Asynchronous programming is a form of concurrency in which operations are executed without blocking the calling thread, typically by representing ongoing work as tasks that can be awaited or completed later. Unlike multithreading, asynchronous programming does not require a dedicated thread for each concurrent operation.

oversimplification_error_explanation: The explanation states that async is 'more like fire-and-forget', which is factually incorrect. ground_truth: To preserve data integrity, a database system must ensure: Atomicity—either all operations of a transaction are reflected in the database or none are; Consistency—a committed transaction preserves all defined integrity constraints, moving the database from one valid state to another; Isolation—concurrent transactions execute without interfering with each other, as if executed serially, with intermediate results hidden; Durability—once a transaction commits, its changes persist despite system failures. Consistency refers to maintaining database integrity rules, while Isolation refers to controlling interaction between concurrent transactions.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 17: Transactions.
strategic_misconception_explanation: It defines Isolation as strictly serial execution ('Only one person can change something at a time'), ignoring that modern databases use concurrency control (like MVCC) to allow concurrent reads/writes without locking everything, which is a key aspect of Isolation.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The 'bathroom' analogy for Isolation implies mutual exclusion (locking) is the only way to achieve isolation, misleading learners into thinking concurrent access is impossible or always requires blocking, whereas isolation levels like Read Committed allow concurrent access.

ground_truth: Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes contain atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups. Second Normal Form (2NF): The relation is in 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): The relation is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies; non-key attributes depend only on candidate keys. Normalization to 3NF eliminates common insertion, update, and deletion anomalies and is widely considered a practical design goal, although higher normal forms (e.g., BCNF) may be required in some cases.
reference: Date, C. J. (2004). An Introduction to Database Systems (8th ed.). Pearson/Addison Wesley, Chapter 12: Further Normalization I: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, pp. 349–388.

ground_truth: The SQL JOIN clause combines rows from two or more tables based on a specified join condition. INNER JOIN returns only rows for which the join condition evaluates to true in both tables. LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the right table are set to NULL. RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table; for non-matching rows, attributes from the left table are set to NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables; rows are matched where the join condition holds, and non-matching rows from either side are padded with NULL values.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 6.3.6–6.3.8: SQL Join Expressions and Outerjoins.

concept: Indexes: When a B-tree index does not speed up a query
ground_truth: A B-tree index may not be used or may not improve query performance when the query has low selectivity (i.e., it returns a large fraction of the table), in which case a full table scan can be more efficient than index-based access due to the cost of random disk I/O. The index may also be ineffective if the query applies functions, expressions, or negation to the indexed column, preventing efficient index lookup, or if the table is very small. Database query optimizers use cost-based analysis and table statistics to determine whether to use an index.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson, Chapter 14: Index Structures. / Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 14: Indexing.

concept: Transactions: Different isolation levels (Read Committed vs Serializable)
ground_truth: READ COMMITTED ensures that a transaction reads only data that has been committed by other transactions; however, successive reads within the same transaction may return different results, allowing non-repeatable reads and phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE ensures that concurrent transactions execute with results equivalent to some serial schedule, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation levels improve correctness guarantees but typically reduce concurrency.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 17: Transactions.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly states that in Read Committed, a friend might see an 'old number' (uncommitted data) while another transaction is writing. Read Committed prevents dirty reads, meaning one transaction cannot read uncommitted data from another.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy of seeing an 'old number' or 'flicker' implies reading uncommitted data, which contradicts the definition of Read Committed. This misleads the learner about the fundamental guarantee of the isolation level.

ground_truth: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability. Consistency means that all nodes see the same data at the same time (i.e., every read reflects the most recent write). Availability means that every request receives a response, regardless of the state of individual nodes. Partition tolerance means that the system continues to operate despite network partitions (communication failures between nodes). Since network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, CAP is commonly interpreted as a trade-off between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) under partition conditions.
reference: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill, Chapter 19: Distributed Databases.
dangerous_analogy_explanation: The analogy implies that consistency and availability are mutually exclusive in a way that suggests you must sacrifice one entirely to get the other, whereas in practice, systems often balance them (e.g., eventual consistency). However, for a simplified explanation of the trade-off, this is acceptable. The statement 'If you really want 100% consistency... you might have to slow down' is slightly misleading as it conflates latency with availability, but it captures the essence of the trade-off under partition. The core error is in the summary table which lists 'Speed or availability' as what you give up for Consistency, which is imprecise but not a strategic misconception about the theorem itself. The biggest issue is the claim 'Most apps pick availability + partition tolerance' as a universal truth, which is a generalization, not an error. The analogy of the oven breaking under pressure for consistency is a bit loose but not fundamentally wrong in the context of CAP (CP systems often reject requests or wait, appearing 'slow' or 'unavailable' to the user). I will flag the oversimplification regarding the nature of the trade-off.
oversimplification_error_explanation: The explanation simplifies the trade-off to 'Consistency vs Availability' under partition, which is correct. However, it states 'If you really want 100% consistency... you might have to slow down'. In CAP, 'slow down' is not the trade-off; the trade-off is Availability (rejecting requests) or Consistency (waiting). Latency is a performance metric, not the binary choice of CAP. This is a minor imprecision.

concept: Denormalization: When and why to use it
ground_truth: Denormalization is the process of intentionally introducing redundancy into a normalized relational schema to improve read performance by reducing the need for join operations. It is a deliberate trade-off, commonly used in read-heavy workloads (e.g., reporting or data warehousing), where the cost of joins outweighs the overhead of maintaining redundant data. While denormalization can significantly accelerate SELECT queries, it increases storage requirements, complicates write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and introduces the risk of data inconsistency due to redundant representations.
reference: Garcia-Molina, H., Ullman, J. D., & Widom, J. (2009). Database Systems: The Complete Book (2nd ed.). Pearson. / Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2019). Database System Concepts (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill.

ground_truth: The TCP three-way handshake establishes a connection and synchronizes sequence numbers between client and server. (1) The client sends a TCP segment with the SYN flag set and a pseudo-random initial sequence number (client_isn), entering the SYN_SENT state. (2) The server responds with a SYN-ACK segment containing its own pseudo-random initial sequence number (server_isn) and an acknowledgment number of client_isn+1, entering the SYN_RCVD state. (3) The client replies with an ACK segment with acknowledgment number server_isn+1. Both sides then transition to the ESTABLISHED state. The handshake confirms bidirectional communication and initializes sequence number spaces for reliable data transfer.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 3.5: TCP Connection Management, pp. 240–246.

concept: OSI model vs TCP/IP model (differences in layers)
ground_truth: The OSI model defines a seven-layer architecture: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application. The TCP/IP model defines a four-layer architecture: Link (Network Interface), Internet, Transport, and Application. The TCP/IP model consolidates the OSI Physical and Data Link layers into the Link layer, and the OSI Session and Presentation layers into the Application layer. While the OSI model serves as a conceptual reference framework, the TCP/IP model reflects the practical architecture of the Internet protocol suite.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 1.5

ground_truth: DNS resolution can be recursive or iterative. In recursive resolution, a DNS server resolves the query on behalf of the client, contacting other servers as needed and returning the final answer. In iterative resolution, each DNS server returns the best information it has (often a referral), and the client (or resolver) continues querying other servers. Recursive queries shift the resolution burden to the server, while iterative queries distribute it across multiple queries.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson,Chapter 2.4: DNS, pp. 168–175.
strategic_misconception_explanation: It incorrectly states that iterative resolution is 'Most Common' for regular DNS lookups and that it is 'Used by DNS resolvers... to forward queries'. In standard DNS architecture, the client sends a recursive query to a resolver, and the resolver performs iterative queries to other servers. The client does not perform iterative resolution; the resolver does. This misattributes the iterative process to the client/resolver relationship rather than the server-to-server hierarchy.

ground_truth: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) represents IP addresses using a prefix of arbitrary length, written as a.b.c.d/x, where x indicates the number of bits in the network portion. CIDR enables flexible subnetting and efficient allocation of IP address space by eliminating fixed class boundaries. Routers use the longest prefix match rule to determine the forwarding path for a packet.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 4.4: IP Addressing, pp. 330–336

concept: HTTP methods: Idempotency of GET, PUT, DELETE versus POST
ground_truth: HTTP methods differ in semantics and idempotency. A method is idempotent if multiple identical requests have the same effect as a single request. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeated requests do not change the result beyond the initial application. POST is not idempotent, as repeated requests can create multiple resources or cause repeated side effects. Idempotency is important for reliability and retry mechanisms in distributed systems.

concept: Routing: Distance Vector (RIP) vs Link State (OSPF)
ground_truth: Distance-vector routing algorithms (e.g., RIP) compute shortest paths based on information from neighboring routers, iteratively updating distance estimates using distributed Bellman-Ford equations. Link-state routing algorithms (e.g., OSPF) require each router to have a complete view of the network topology and compute shortest paths using Dijkstra’s algorithm. Distance-vector approaches are simpler but slower to converge and susceptible to routing loops, while link-state approaches converge faster and provide more accurate routing at the cost of higher complexity.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 5.3–5.4: Routing Algorithms, pp. 365–385.
strategic_misconception_explanation: The explanation incorrectly states that Link State routing is 'Impossible' to have loops because every router has a complete view. While LS algorithms prevent loops during convergence if implemented correctly, the statement is an overgeneralization; more critically, it mischaracterizes the update mechanism as 'Triggered' for OSPF without mentioning the periodic flooding of LSAs (every 30 mins or upon change), which is a key operational detail. However, the most significant error is in the 'Key Differences' table where it claims OSPF updates are 'Triggered (only when topology changes)' while RIP is 'Periodic'. OSPF does use triggered updates for LSAs, but it also has a refresh timer. This is a minor nuance. The bigger issue is the claim that OSPF has 'No loops' as an absolute feature of the algorithm itself, whereas loop prevention is a result of the synchronized state, not just the algorithm. But the most glaring error is in the 'Practical Example' for RIP: It says 'A tells B: I know C is 1 hop away via you' and then 'B tells A: I know C is 0 hops away'. This implies B is directly connected to C. Then it calculates A's distance as B's distance (0) + 1 = 1. This is actually correct for a 2-hop path (A-B-C). Wait, the text says 'A thinks C is 1 hop away... but B's cost to C is 3'. This is a contradiction. If B is directly connected to C, the cost is 1 (or whatever the link cost is). If the cost is 3, B is not directly connected in the sense of a single hop in RIP (which counts hops, not cost). RIP uses hop count. If A-B is 1 hop and B-C is 1 hop, A-C is 2 hops. The example confuses 'cost' (OSPF metric) with 'hop count' (RIP metric). It states 'B's cost to C is 3' in the OSPF section, then applies it to RIP, saying 'RIP only knows hop count, not the actual path cost'. This is a category error in the example. It mixes OSPF costs into a RIP explanation. This is a significant factual error in the illustrative example.

concept: TLS handshake (RSA vs Diffie-Hellman key exchange)
ground_truth: TLS handshake protocols establish a secure connection by negotiating cryptographic parameters and exchanging keys. In RSA-based key exchange, the client encrypts a premaster secret with the server’s public key, allowing the server to derive the session keys. In Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, both parties contribute to a shared secret without transmitting it directly, providing forward secrecy. Modern TLS implementations prefer (EC)DHE over RSA key exchange due to improved security properties.
reference: Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2020). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson, Chapter 8.3: Secure Sockets Layer / TLS, pp. 712–720.

ground_truth: Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm whose running time depends on the balance of partitioning. In the worst case, it runs in Θ(n²), when the partition produces subproblems of sizes n−1 and 0. Under the assumption that all elements are distinct and all permutations are equally likely, its expected running time is Θ(n log n). The algorithm sorts in place and uses additional space proportional to the recursion depth.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, pp. 182–184.

ground_truth: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem on a weighted directed graph with nonnegative edge weights. It maintains a set of vertices whose shortest-path distances from the source have been finalized and repeatedly selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance using a priority queue, then relaxes its outgoing edges. Correctness relies on the property that once a vertex is extracted, its shortest-path distance is final, which holds only when all edge weights are nonnegative.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Section 22.3, pp 604 - 645.

strategic_misconception_explanation: The example scenario provided to illustrate the failure of Dijkstra's algorithm is factually incorrect. It claims that with edges A->B (1) and B->C (-2), the path via B has cost -1, and a direct edge A->C (0) would be finalized first. In reality, Dijkstra's algorithm would extract A (dist 0), then B (dist 1), then C (dist -1). If the direct edge A->C (0) existed, it would be relaxed when processing A, setting C's tentative distance to 0. When B is processed, it updates C to -1. Since -1 < 0, the final distance is -1. The algorithm actually produces the correct shortest path in this specific graph structure because the negative edge is on the path to the node being finalized later, not one that invalidates a previously finalized node's distance in a way that breaks the logic described. A better counter-example involves a negative edge on a path to a node that was already finalized as having a shorter positive distance, which Dijkstra fails to update. The provided example is misleading because it describes a scenario where Dijkstra might actually work or where the logic described doesn't match the algorithm's execution trace.

ground_truth: A hash table maps keys to array slots. A collision occurs when two or more keys hash to the same slot. The load factor α = N/M is the ratio of stored elements to table size. As α increases, the probability of collisions increases and performance degrades. Under uniform hashing and open addressing, the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is approximately 1/(1−α).
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press, Chapter 11, pp 272 - 311.

concept: Binary search tree balancing (AVL vs Red-Black)
ground_truth: An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. This strict balance ensures O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, but may require more rotations during updates. A red-black tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains balance using color-based properties (red and black nodes), guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case time for search, insertion, and deletion, typically with fewer rotations than AVL trees at the cost of a potentially higher tree height.
reference: Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2022). Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.). MIT Press. AVL trees: Problem 13-3, pp. 358–360. Red-black trees: Chapter 13, pp. 331–359.
